newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: PRESS DIGEST - CENTRAL AND EAST EUROPE - DEC 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - CENTRAL AND EAST EUROPE - DEC 4.

text.p: AUSTRIA
DER STANDARD
- The government coalition has agreed to let family- owned shops open on Sundays. All other shops will be allowed to open on Saturday afternoons and until 7.30 p.m. on weekdays.
- In November 234,505 Austrians were unemployed, 2,696 more than the same period a year ago.
- tele.ring, the telecommunications company of energy provider Verbund and federal railways OeBB, plans to provide data-communications for big companies by 1997.
- Skimaker Fischer's aircraft supplier Fischer Advanced Composite Components has won an order worth 100 million schillings to make wing parts for Boeing's new 737 generation.
- The conservative junior coalition partner has blocked a planned tax increase on trucks by social democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima. Social Democrats have threatened counter-measures.
- Benetton's restaurant unit Autogrill wants to take over Austria's motorway restaurant chain Wienerwald.
DIE PRESSE
- By 1997 the decline in the number of tourists visiting Austria should slow down, research institute IHS says.

- Early retirement is having an impact on the number of workers in the population. Austria no longer has one of the highest rates of employment among its potential workforce, a study by the International Labour Organisation shows.
KURIER
- Trade unions are threatening not to support the introduction of Europe's single currency euro, if a chapter on labour is not added to the Maastricht-treaty.
- New rumours on the privatisation of Creditanstalt present Credit Suisse again as a potential bidder.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- British chemical giant Courtaulds and Austria's fibremaker Lenzing have cancelled plans for a joint-venture in the United States.
- Austria's central bank will loose 800 million schillings because of the European Monetary Union.
SLOVAKIA

HOSPODARSKE NOVINY - The Association of Security Traders has sent an open letter to parliament asking it to reject the new securities law returned by the President last month. They say the law will have a negative effect on the capital market.

- Rating agency Standard and Poors has given a "pi" rating to five banks, while three received the "BBpi" rating and two "Bpi". The agency added that the banking sector still has many problems to solve.
- The government has approved a draft law limiting imports of goods which are also produced in Slovakia. The new law should take effect on July 1, 1997.
- Exporters and importers will have to contribute 0.05 percent of their foreign trade volume to the new ExIm bank which is to be set up next year.

PRAVDA - Frantisek Gaulieder, the parliamentarian who quit the ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), denied that he had sent a letter to the chairman of parliament announcing he was resigning his mandate.
- The central bank says that according to its calculations, next year's budget will have a fiscal deficit of 24.7 billion crowns, which is 3.7 percent of the gross domestic product.

- The parliamentary opposition is opposed to the draft budget to be presented to parliament later this week because it does not cover the basic needs of individual ministries and has few impulses for further economic development.

PRACA - The Union of Slovak Towns has called on its members - the mayors of towns and villages - to protest against cuts to local budgets planned in the draft budget. The protest is to take place outside parliament on Wednesday.

NARODNA OBRODA - Agriculture ministers from CEFTA nations will meet in Bratislava on Wednesday to discuss further cooperation in the fields of food protection, veterinary cooperation, trade policies in the lumber sector and commercial relations.
- The government on Tuesday approved the new draft of the penal code proposed by a group of coalition members of parliament.
SLOVENSKA REPUBLIKA - President Michal Kovac will give a state of the nation address to parliament on December 11.
- Former HDS deputy Frantisek Gaulieder has resigned his mandate, after previously he would stay on as an independent member of parliament.
LATVIA
ALL NEWSPAPERS

- Deputy Janis Adamsons, who has proposed a parliamentary committee to investigate the activities of the Latvian Savings Bank and Unibanka, thinks that as a result of the investigation "somebody" will be brought to justice. It is not clear whether parliament will set up the commission.

- Parliament's committee for human rights and public affairs, the interior ministry and the president's office are drawing up an amnesty law. Some 20 percent of Latvia's 10,000 prison inmates will be subject to the amnesty.

- At the Lisbon OSCE conference, President Guntis Ulmanis said the functioning of the Skrunda radar station will expire in 1998 and it will have to be demolished. He called an anchievement the fact that no international organisation talks about the existence of a human rights problem in Latvia.
DIENA
- Customs authorities in Riga are to confiscate some of the 2.15 million litres of alcohol seized by the British company Crown Agents, which is helping the Latvian Customs.
NEATKARIGA RITA AVIZE

- Scandinavian ministers for immigration decided that their countries will provide asylum to 108 refugees from the refugee camp in Olaine. They said this was an extraordinary step and hoped that Latvian legislation will be brougt into line with the 1951 Convention on refugees.
BIZNES & BALTIYA
- Judging by recent statements by Latvian officials, no radical turn is to be expected in talks on the Russian-Latvian border, the newsaper says.
DIENAS BIZNESS
- The creditors of Banka Baltija were unhappy with the auction that was held to sell off the bank's assets.
CROATIA
VJESNIK
- President Tudjman made a surprise visit on Tuesday to the war-ravaged eastern Croatian town Vukovar, currently under U.N. Transitional Administration control.
- Money market: Liquidity improves.
- Employers's association warns it will ask government to indemnify their companies for losses suffered due to the rail strike.
VECERNJI LIST
- Croatian railway traffic at a standstill: The railway workers' strike has ground to a halt virtually all services as of early Tuesday morning, causing huge losses in the Croatian economy.
- Figures for the first nine months of 1996 show the cost of living in the Croatian capital Zagreb has gone up exactly 4.7 percent year-on-year.

- The Plomin Two thermo-electric plant will not be a polluter as all waste materials will be put to good use, says the general manager of the Croatian power company HEP, reacting to allegations to the contrary.
- Foreign consultants hired to design the restructuring of public companies object to the state railways (HZ) being viewed as a "provider of services" rather than a commercial company.
SLOBODNA DALMACIJA
- Rumour has it that local elections and those for the House of Counties will be held on March 16, 1997, while presidential elections may be scheduled for late summer next year.
- Pope John Paul II may visit Sarajevo on April 13, 1997, combining it with his visit to Prague.

- High price of capital poses a threat to economy, says director of the Zagreb money market, Josip Gotovac, in an interview. He says interest rates could be cut from the current 18-25 pct in a joint effort of the government and banks.

- Total first half operating losses of the banking sector put at 18.1 million kuna, compared to a profit of 52.8 million kuna in the same period of 1995, according to a report of the central payments bureau ZAP.
